```{r first-code}
2 + 2

sample_count <- 8

```

R is case-sensitive: `sample_count` and `Sample_count` are different objects.
Try running `Sample_count` below — it should error. Read the error message
before moving on; most R errors tell you exactly what went wrong.


# R Basic Programming

## Objects and types

```{r object-types}
gene_name      <- "BRCA1"   # character - always quoted
expr_value     <- 42.7      # numeric
is_significant <- TRUE      # logical - no quotes

class(gene_name)
class(expr_value)
class(is_significant)
```

## Vectors

A vector is one measurement type repeated — think of it as one gene's
expression across several samples.

```{r vectors}
brca1 <- c(120, 95, 143, 88, 310, 287, 340, 295)
brca1

length(brca1)
mean(brca1)
summary(brca1)
```

**Vectorisation.** R applies an operation to every element at once — this is
why R feels natural for expression data with thousands of genes.

```{r vectorisation}
log_brca1 <- log2(brca1 + 1)
log_brca1
```

**Subsetting.**

```{r subsetting}
brca1[1]        # first sample
brca1[c(1, 2)]  # first two
brca1[-1]       # everything EXCEPT the first
```

**Logical subsetting — the gene-filtering pattern.** You write a condition, R
returns `TRUE`/`FALSE` for each element, and that mask selects. This pattern
reappears constantly for the rest of the course.

```{r logical-subsetting}
brca1 > 200          # a logical mask
brca1[brca1 > 200]   # keep only where TRUE
sum(brca1 > 200)     # count how many passed
```

Missing values are coded `NA`. `mean()` returns `NA` unless you tell it to
ignore missing values:

```{r na-handling}
expr <- c(120, 95, NA, 88)
mean(expr)
mean(expr, na.rm = TRUE)
```

## Factors

A factor is a character vector with a fixed set of allowed values — an
experimental group.

```{r factors}
condition <- c("control", "control", "control", "control",
               "treated", "treated", "treated", "treated")
condition <- factor(condition, levels = c("control", "treated"))
condition
levels(condition)
table(condition)
```

The **first level is the reference/baseline** in every comparison R makes.
Setting it explicitly (as above) prevents a whole class of "my results are
backwards" bugs later.

## Data frames

A data frame is a table where every column is a vector of the same length —
the sample metadata sheet.

```{r data-frames}
metadata <- data.frame(
  sample_id = c("S1", "S2", "S3", "S4", "S5", "S6", "S7", "S8"),
  condition = condition,
  batch     = c(1, 1, 2, 2, 1, 1, 2, 2)
)

metadata
dim(metadata)
str(metadata)
```

```{r access-df}
metadata$condition                          # one column, by name
metadata[metadata$batch == 2, ]             # logical subsetting on rows
```

# Data Manipulation using `tidyverse`

What you have learned above also can be called as base R, means one line do specific task and you need to define it all the time.

R has the easier way - using a library called `tidyverse`. `Tidyverse` also provides the aggregation method such as group_by or aggregation.

```{r ex-r-base}

# Load mpg dataset from ggplot2 library
mpg

# Base R is built for stability, particularly for production-level script
audi <- mpg
audi_subset <- subset(audi, manufacturer == "audi" & year == 1999)
audi$new_column <- "new_column"
audi_subset

```

```{r ex-tidyverse}

# Load mpg dataset from ggplot2 library
mpg

# Tidyverse offers direct, human readable form
# %>% is the pipe operator, you can read the command as "followed by"
audi_tidy <- mpg %>%
  filter(manufacturer == "audi", year == 1999) %>%
  mutate(new_column = "new_column")
audi_tidy

```

Tidyverse is quite good when we handle complex situation, such as filter and then do some agglomeration function.

```{r ex-tidyverse-complex}

# Load mpg dataset from ggplot2 library
mpg

# Tidyverse offers direct, human readable form
# %>% is the pipe operator, you can read the command as "followed by"
audi_get_high_engine <- mpg %>%
  filter(manufacturer == "audi") %>%
  mutate(new_column = "new_column") %>%
  arrange(desc(displ)) %>%
  select(model, displ, year)
audi_get_high_engine

```

# Saving your processed data in R

All your work needs to be saved, otherwise you need to make it since R only save the data in environment when computer is active.

There are several ways to save your data in R, such as TXT/TSV/CSV, Excel file, or RDS (R Dataset).

```{r save-data}

# Save based on TSV/TXT

write_delim(audi_get_high_engine,
            paste0("/Users/hakimbazol/Documents/audi_get_high_engine.tsv"),
            delim = "\t")

# Save based on CSV

write_delim(audi_get_high_engine,
            paste0("/Users/hakimbazol/Documents/audi_get_high_engine.csv"),
            delim = ",")

# Save based on Excel

write_xlsx(audi_get_high_engine,
            paste0("/Users/hakimbazol/Documents/audi_get_high_engine.xlsx")
)

# Save based on RDS

saveRDS(audi_get_high_engine,
            paste0("/Users/hakimbazol/Documents/audi_get_high_engine.rds"))
```

Additional step : Read RDS file

```{r open-rds}

# open RDS file

audi_rds <- readRDS("/Users/hakimbazol/Documents/audi_get_high_engine.rds") 
audi_rds

```
